cells.tense: You sit here with the pen and the exchange is level.
cells.ask: Pick an arrangement in your life where the give and take still works, and set its shape somewhere it stands when your hand comes off it.
cells.core:
There is an exchange in your life that currently balances, and you can feel it working. Nobody is quietly carrying more than their share, and you are not keeping a tally in your head to make sure. The fairness runs by itself, which means it did not get there by accident. It got there because something in you can tell what is even and what is not, and you have been listening to it.

The openness is the point. Nothing has hardened into a fixed arrangement yet, so take one of the balanced exchanges that is already holding and give it a shape that lasts after you stop watching — a note, a habit, a split you do not re-decide each time. That is what this wants next, not more generosity: some steady form for what is already fair.
cells.sheetLine: What is even here holds without your watching it.
cells.verb: weighing what is given against what comes back
cells.place: the open ground before anything has been chosen or refused

cells.tense: You are already auditing an exchange that has not happened yet.
cells.act: carry your own share, all of it
cells.ask: For one week, carry only what is yours and count nothing — not what anyone owes, not what you are owed. Anything left over, handle once at the close.
cells.core:
You are keeping accounts on something that has not been created yet. Before the exchange exists, the book is open: who will give what, who will fall short, what you will be owed when this is real. The fairness you want is real, but you are applying it to a balance that has not happened, so the counting does not close.

For one week, carry your own share all the way through and leave the rest uncounted. You will feel the pull to check — that someone gives less, that you will end up short. Let it be. In seven days you will see, without having watched, whether anything actually went wrong. Most of it will not have. What did, you handle once, then, rather than each day.

cells.tense: You are at a door whose hinge has already turned.
cells.act: sort what matters from what does not, carefully
cells.ask: Take one stretch of your time and split it: what you gave freely, what you gave out of obligation. Drop one item from the second pile this week.
cells.core:
The mutual part has gone quiet where you are. Handing things over still works — you can pass them along without hesitation. What comes toward you does not land the same way, and offers that arrive seem to pass through. The account stays on one side, and you keep it there.

Sort one honest stretch of your time. Not your whole life — one week, one project, the last month of something. Put what you gave freely in one column, what you gave because it was required in another. Then drop one item from the second column. An hour comes back, maybe two. Keep that hour and spend it on something that resembles nothing owed, so a portion of the exchange finally returns to you.

cells.tense: You keep something even and have not signed your name to it.
cells.act: hold two true things without declaring either
cells.ask: When something next feels off-balance, weigh both sides quietly before you act, then do whatever you were going to do.
cells.core:
A situation tips and something in you registers it before you can argue for it — who carries too much, what would make it fair again. That reading does its work on you. What is missing is your name on it. You put it down to circumstances being what they are, or other people being reasonable, or the situation sorting itself out.

You do not need to announce anything. The next time something feels unbalanced, weigh both sides quietly before you do anything about it. Let the call be yours first. Then adjust, wait, speak, or leave it — whichever you were going to do. Someone who keeps a balance instead of only feeling it does one extra thing: they hold the read as theirs. You are already keeping it. Only the signature is missing.

The sentence that serves me more than them would be any line naming a counterpart who is being kept waiting, given more than they give, or owed — I've cut all of those.
